findings.reason: The authentic original standalone tiles show an entirely prose-based colored insertion/deletion construction. A concrete pair of multitableaux materially clarifies which entries are permutation values and which are global recording times, and how color controls the component. The new example includes both a genuine bump and a nontrivial reverse deletion. This is a warranted explanatory diagram under the expanded editorial criterion, rather than a claim that the existing proof is incomplete.

diagram_math_checks.details: The input is a permutation of 1,2,3,4 with colors 1,2,1,2. Step 1.1 routes positions 1 and 3 to component 1, giving value word (4,3), and positions 2 and 4 to component 2, giving (1,2). The displayed arrow denotes this forward algorithm, not an additional morphism.

At i=1: P1=[4],Q1=[1]. At i=2: P2=[1],Q2=[2]. At i=3, inserting 3 into [4] bumps 4 to row 2, so P1=[3;4], while recording time 3 is placed below 1, giving Q1=[1;3]. At i=4, inserting 2 into [1] appends it, giving P2=[1,2],Q2=[2,4]. These are the eight exact entries drawn.

Both multitableaux have first component partition (1,1) and second component (2). P1 has 3<4 down its column, Q1 has 1<3 down its column, and P2,Q2 have 1<2 and 2<4 across rows. Each of P and Q contains 1,2,3,4 exactly once across components, as required by F2 and the local supplier definition.

By step 1.2, time 4 removes the right corner of Q2 and expels 2 from P2. Time 3 removes the bottom corner of Q1; reverse deletion starts with 4, exchanges it with the rightmost smaller entry 3 in the row above, and expels 3, leaving P1=[4]. Times 2 and 1 then expel 1 from component 2 and 4 from component 1. Recovered descending-time pairs are (2,2),(3,1),(1,2),(4,1). A direct local Python computation of insertion and reverse deletion independently reproduced every intermediate state and asserted all four recovered input pairs.

Only the existing algorithms of steps 1.1–2.1 and standard multitableau definition F2 are illustrated. The square-count proof in step 3.1 remains unchanged and independent of the figure; the picture does not assert that this one example establishes the bijection.
